issues.title: No way to declare the reference frame a vector quantity is resolved in
issues.author: clemensv
issues.body:
# The gap

`coordinateReferenceSystem` binds the members that give a **position**. There is
no way to state the reference frame that the components of a **vector quantity**
are resolved in, and a vector quantity is not a position.

The keyword's normative text is about locating a point. §"The
`coordinateReferenceSystem` Keyword" says it identifies the system "under which
coordinate values held in properties of an object or tuple are to be
interpreted", §"The `reference` Property" requires a CRS "whose definition
establishes an ordered set of axes, each with an axis direction and unit of
measure", and §"The `coordinates` Property" requires that "the number of names
MUST equal the dimension of that coordinate system". A magnetic field vector has
three components resolved on three axes, but it does not locate anything, and
the record that carries it usually also carries the position at which it was
measured. Reading the keyword to cover both would make "the coordinate" of such
a record ambiguous.

The at-most-one rule closes the door on the obvious workaround:

> An object or tuple MUST NOT carry more than one `coordinateReferenceSystem`
> annotation.

A solar wind record carries a spacecraft position **and** a field vector **and**
a velocity vector, all resolved in the same or in different frames. Under the
current rule at most one of the three can be annotated, and the nesting advice
that follows the rule does not help, because upstream feeds publish these as
flat sibling members and the samples are meant to annotate the shape the
publisher actually emits.

Nothing else in the document covers it either: `unit` and `symbol` give the
magnitude of each component, `semanticRole` says each is an `observationValue`,
`concepts` can name the observed property — but none of them says that `hp`,
`hn` and `he` are one quantity rather than three, nor which way each axis
points.

# Where it bites

Two samples in this repository.

**`samples/real-world/20-goes-magnetometer`** — the NOAA SWPC GOES magnetometer
publishes `hp`, `hn` and `he`: the components of the magnetic field in a
spacecraft-local triad, where `hp` is parallel to the Earth's dipole axis and
positive northward, `hn` lies along the spacecraft–Earth line and is positive
earthward, and `he` completes the triad perpendicular to both and is positive
eastward. Every one of those facts is currently stated in the schema's prose
`description`, because there is no keyword to put it in. The schema says so
explicitly:

> The frame in which the components are resolved is stated in prose here,
> because the coordinate reference system annotation binds the members that give
> a position and not the members that give the components of a vector.

**Solar wind magnetometry** (`bx_gsm`, `by_gsm`, `bz_gsm`) is the same shape,
with the added wrinkle that the frame is named in the member names and nowhere
else. `bz_gsm` going negative is the single most consequential quantity in
operational space weather, and it is consequential *only* because GSM's z axis
is aligned with the geomagnetic dipole — which the schema cannot say.

The pattern is not confined to space physics. Accelerometer and gyroscope
triads, wind components (u/v/w), current velocity components resolved on an
instrument frame, and stress or strain tensors all have it.

# What a consumer loses

Without the frame:

- Two records cannot be compared. GOES-16 and GOES-19 resolve `hp`/`hn`/`he` in
  different physical directions because they are stationed at different
  longitudes. Nothing in either schema says the members are not interchangeable.
- The magnitude cannot be checked against the components, because a consumer
  cannot tell whether the triad is orthogonal.
- The vector cannot be transformed into another frame, which is the first thing
  any analysis does.
- A consumer cannot tell a three-component vector from three unrelated
  scalars that happen to share a prefix.

# Proposal

Add a `vectorReferenceFrame` keyword that reuses the shape of
`coordinateReferenceSystem` and differs from it in exactly the two places where
a vector differs from a position.

```json
{
  "name": "GoesMagnetometer",
  "type": "object",
  "vectorReferenceFrame": {
    "reference": "#/definitions/GoesEpnFrame",
    "kind": "type",
    "components": ["hp", "hn", "he"]
  },
  "properties": {
    "hp": { "type": "double", "unit": "nT" },
    "hn": { "type": "double", "unit": "nT" },
    "he": { "type": "double", "unit": "nT" }
  }
}
```

- `reference` and `kind` keep their meaning and their value space unchanged. The
  existing `type` kind already does most of the work: a `tuple` meta-type whose
  elements in order are the axes, each carrying its unit, with direction and
  origin stated in the element `description`s, is precisely how an unregistered
  vector frame is written down. That machinery exists; it is only forbidden from
  being used for something that is not a position.
- `components` replaces `coordinates`. Same rules — a non-empty ordered array of
  distinct direct property names, numeric types, count equal to the dimension of
  the frame, units compatible with the axes, ordering asserted by the author and
  not inferred.
- **An object MAY carry more than one `vectorReferenceFrame`**, because a record
  may carry more than one vector quantity, and it may carry a
  `coordinateReferenceSystem` at the same time. The two annotations bind
  disjoint sets of members; overlap between any two of them on one object should
  be forbidden.

A registered vocabulary exists for the heliophysics cases: the SPASE data model
enumerates the standard frames (GSE, GSM, GEI, SM, RTN, and others), so a
`spase-frame` kind, or whatever it should be called after checking what SPASE
actually serves, would cover the solar wind sample without a hand-written
meta-type. The GOES spacecraft triad is not registered anywhere and would use
`kind: "type"`.

## Alternatives considered

**Relax `coordinateReferenceSystem` instead.** Drop the at-most-one rule and add
a discriminator, say `quantity: "position" | "vector"`. This is a smaller delta
to the document, but it overloads a keyword whose name, prose, and ISO 19111
reference are all about coordinates, and it makes every existing consumer that
assumed one CRS per object wrong. A separate keyword leaves
`coordinateReferenceSystem` and everything already written against it untouched.

**Do nothing, and say so.** If vector frames are deliberately out of scope, the
document should say that in the Scope section or in the
`coordinateReferenceSystem` section, so that a schema author who reaches for it
and finds it does not fit learns why. That is strictly better than the present
silence, but it leaves a common shape of observational record — arguably the
most common one in geophysics after the scalar time series — with no annotation
at all.

# Related

- json-structure/core#30, which is about a different limitation on the same
  sample: `unit` cannot be attached to a nullable union, so the optional
  channels in these feeds have to be modelled as non-nullable and omitted from
  `required`.

issues.title: Consider a keyword for rank-2 tensor (matrix) quantities bound to reference frames
issues.author: clemensv
issues.body:
## Question

`vectorReferenceFrames` binds an ordered set of members to the axes of a named frame. Rank-2 tensor quantities (matrices) have the same problem and are not covered. Should the extension define a keyword for them?

## Why it is the same problem

The components of a tensor are meaningless apart from the frame, the component order is not inferable from property names, and the conventions in circulation genuinely conflict. Three candidate real-world cases:

- **Transformation matrix.** The OPC UA / OpenUSD binding draft §7.4.2 pins `xformOp:transform` (`matrix4d`) to "row-major, row-vector pre-multiplication (`v' = v · M`), the upper-left 3x3 being `R`, and the translation in the fourth row." Row-major vs column-major combined with pre- vs post-multiplication is the canonical graphics interop bug, and the fact that a binding spec has to state it normatively is the evidence that it is not inferable. **Source: `marcschier/opcua-drafts`, `metaverse-specs/openusd-binding/OPC-UA-OpenUSD-Bindings.md` §7.4.2 — a working-group draft, not a ratified standard, so it demonstrates the ambiguity rather than settling it.**
- **Seismic moment tensor.** GCMT and USGS ComCat publish `Mrr, Mtt, Mpp, Mrt, Mrp, Mtp`. The component names are conventionally read against a spherical up-south-east frame, while the Aki-Richards convention is north-east-down. Choosing the wrong one flips signs on the off-diagonal terms, and nothing in the payload says which is meant. **Sources to be verified against the GCMT and USGS product documentation before drafting.**
- **State covariance matrix.** CCSDS OPM/OEM carry a 6x6 covariance for a position-velocity state, expressed in a stated frame such as RTN or an inertial frame. **Source to be verified against the CCSDS blue books.**

Neither of the latter two is currently in the sample set. Sample 05 is a JMA bulletin and carries no tensor.

## Why it is not a small addition

A rank-2 tensor is indexed by a *pair* of axes, so the flat ordered `components` array of `vectorReferenceFrames` cannot express it. A nested row-major array of member names would, but that raises four questions the vector keyword never had to answer.

1. **Storage layout.** Row-major vs column-major, and whether the convention is pre- or post-multiplication. The transformation-matrix case above shows both halves of this in one sentence of normative text.
2. **Symmetry.** Publishers report 6 components for a symmetric 3x3, not 9. The schema has to state which is meant, or the reader has to guess.
3. **Packing order.** At least two Voigt-style orderings are in circulation (`xx,yy,zz,yz,xz,xy` and `xx,yy,zz,xy,xz,yz`). A keyword that does not pin this down recreates exactly the ambiguity the extension exists to remove, which would be worse than having no keyword at all.
4. **Two frames.** A Jacobian or transformation matrix has rows in one frame and columns in another. Symmetric tensors do not. The keyword shape has to decide whether that case is in scope or explicitly excluded.

## Correction: symmetry is *not* already expressible

An earlier revision of this issue claimed that the overlap relaxation in b7e92bd made symmetric tensors expressible without further syntax, by naming the same member at `[0][1]` and `[1][0]`. **That was wrong.** The draft says the names within *one* `components` array MUST be distinct; the relaxation applies *across* elements of `vectorReferenceFrames`, not within a single `components` array. A nested row-major `components` would therefore need its own explicit relaxation, which is a decision to make rather than a property to inherit.

The justification prose in "Multiple Frames and Shared Components" is written in vector terms ("the frames share the axis in question") and would need generalizing if this is pursued.

## Not proposing to draft this yet

Every keyword in the extension so far is backed by a real-world sample and a verified authoritative source. That discipline is what caught the GOES axis error. A tensor keyword should get the same treatment, grounded in published data rather than being designed from first principles and given a sample afterwards.

Prerequisites before drafting:

- [ ] Verify the GCMT/USGS moment tensor frame convention against primary documentation
- [ ] Verify the CCSDS covariance frame and ordering against the blue books
- [ ] Decide whether asymmetric two-frame matrices are in scope
- [ ] Decide how storage layout, symmetry and packing are declared
- [ ] Decide whether repeated member names within one nested `components` are legal
- [ ] Add a real-world sample before the section is written

comments.author: clemensv
comments.body: Body edited: removed an incorrect claim that the b7e92bd overlap relaxation already made symmetric tensors expressible (the distinctness rule applies within one \components\ array, so it does not), and added the OpenUSD \matrix4d\ transform case as a third grounding example. See #3 for the orientation half of the same review.

comments.author: clemensv
comments.body:
Done. The keyword is drafted as `tensorReferenceFrames` and is not limited to rank 2: `frames` is an array of frame references whose length is the rank, so rank 3 and above are expressible by the same shape.

Resolutions against the checklist in the issue:

- **GCMT frame convention** — verified against the Global CMT `ndk` format document, which states that `r` is up, `t` is south and `p` is east. The document is now cited in the draft as an informative reference (GCMT-NDK).
- **CCSDS covariance ordering** — moot. Composite-state covariance is out of scope, because its indices do not range over the axes of a reference frame. Filed as #4.
- **Asymmetric two-frame matrices** — in scope. `frames` is ordered, so a rank-2 tensor whose two entries name different frames carries a vector in the second frame to a vector in the first. This covers rotation matrices and Jacobians.
- **Storage layout, symmetry and packing** — layout is carried by array nesting, so row-major against column-major never arises. Packing is carried by a per-component `index` tuple, so competing Voigt orderings need not be distinguished. Symmetry is carried by an optional `symmetry` member, permitted only where `frames` has exactly two entries naming the same frame; higher-rank symmetries are explicitly not expressible, and every carried component of such a tensor must be named individually.
- **Repeated member names within one `components`** — not legal. One `index` must not appear twice, and one property must not be named twice.
- **Real-world sample** — added as `samples/real-world/21-gcmt-moment-tensor`, a Global CMT `ndk` record for the magnitude-5 earthquake beneath El Salvador on 1 January 2005, transcribed from the sample record printed in the format document. It exercises one frame named at both index positions, `symmetry` of `symmetric` so that six published members determine nine components, and the indexed form of `components`.

The `vectorReferenceFrames` keyword is kept beside this one rather than folded into it. Vectors are rank-1 tensors, but at rank 1 the frame's declared axis order already states the binding, so a positional list suffices; merging would triple the size of the most common annotation and would force the commonest case to be declared with a keyword called "tensor". `frames` accordingly requires at least two entries, and the draft says why.

Meta-schema updated with `FrameReference`, `TensorComponent`, `TensorComponents`, `TensorReferenceFrame` and `TensorReferenceFrames`, and the keyword added to both the object and the tuple add-in. `check-annotations.py` gained support for type unions with a scalar alternative and for integer value types, both of which the new definitions are the first in the file to use. All samples pass `validate-characteristics.ps1`.

The remaining scope exclusion is tracked in #4.

issues.title: Consider keywords for orientation quantities (Euler angle triples and quaternions)
issues.author: clemensv
issues.body:
## Question

`vectorReferenceFrames` covers vector quantities. Orientation quantities — Euler angle triples and quaternions — are not covered, and they carry exactly the class of unstated convention the extension exists to make explicit.

## Why it matters

Two concrete conventions from the OPC UA / OpenUSD binding draft, §7.4.2:

**Euler order.** The transform profile pins orientation to ISO 9787 intrinsic Tait-Bryan `z-y'-x''`, that is `R = Rz(C) · Ry(B) · Rx(A)`, and states that a differently ordered rotation op "shall not be substituted by a different Euler order without re-deriving the angles." Three numbers named `roll`, `pitch`, `yaw` do not tell a reader the composition order, and the wrong order silently produces a different orientation.

**Quaternion component order.** The same section mandates reordering from the OPC UA / RSL imaginary-first `(x, y, z, w)` to the USD real-first `(w, x, y, z)`. Four numbers, published both ways by conforming systems, with nothing in the payload that says which packing is meant. This is the GOES magnetometer axis-order failure in a different costume.

**Source: `marcschier/opcua-drafts`, `metaverse-specs/openusd-binding/OPC-UA-OpenUSD-Bindings.md` §7.4.2.** This is a working-group draft rather than a ratified standard, so it is evidence that the ambiguity is real and has to be resolved by hand today — not an authority for any particular convention. RSL is OPC 10000-210 and ISO 9787 is the underlying rotation convention; both should be checked directly before drafting.

## Why `vectorReferenceFrames` is the wrong tool

Not merely insufficient — actively misleading if applied here.

The keyword's own text says a vector's "components are its projections onto the axes of a frame." Roll, pitch and yaw are rotations *about* axes, not projections *onto* them. A schema author who annotates `roll`/`pitch`/`yaw` with `vectorReferenceFrames` produces something that passes every check the extension makes and asserts something false. The unit-consistency rule does not catch it either, since all three members are angles and are trivially mutually convertible.

Quaternions fail structurally rather than semantically: a frame has three axes, `components` length MUST equal the axis count, and the scalar part lies on no axis at all.

## What is not being claimed

Handedness and up-axis are properties of the frame itself, so a frame reference that resolves to an authoritative definition already settles them. The binding draft states them explicitly because it is converting between two systems, not because the source data is ambiguous. Those are not gaps.

## Prerequisites before drafting

Same discipline as every other keyword: a real-world sample and a verified authoritative source first.

- [ ] Verify the ISO 9787 rotation convention against the standard rather than a secondary citation
- [ ] Establish how widely the two quaternion packings actually appear in published data formats
- [ ] Decide whether orientation is one keyword or two (angle triples and quaternions have little in common structurally)
- [ ] Decide whether rotation order is expressed as an enumeration or by reference to an external definition
- [ ] Decide whether intrinsic vs extrinsic is a separate axis of the declaration or folded into the order token
- [ ] Add a real-world sample before any section is written
- [ ] Consider whether the `vectorReferenceFrames` section should say explicitly that it does not apply to rotations, independent of whether an orientation keyword is ever added

That last item is worth doing regardless of the outcome here, since the misuse is easy and currently undetectable.

Related: #2 (rank-2 tensors), which shares the transformation-matrix case from the same source section.

issues.title: tensorReferenceFrames: augmented 4x4 transforms and composite-state covariance are out of scope and now undocumented
issues.author: clemensv
issues.body:
Two things commonly carried as matrices are not expressible by `tensorReferenceFrames` as drafted. The scope paragraph that stated this has been removed from the draft, so the limitation is now undocumented and this issue is the only record of it.

## What is not covered

**1. Augmented homogeneous transformation matrices (4x4).**
The fourth row and column index a homogeneous coordinate, not an axis of a reference frame. `frames` requires one frame reference per index position, and there is no frame whose axes the fourth index ranges over. The 3x3 rotation block *is* expressible where a schema carries it as a member of its own.

This is the OPC UA / OpenUSD `matrix4d` case from #2, and it is one of the motivating cases that prompted the keyword.

**2. Covariance matrices over a composite state.**
A 6x6 position-velocity covariance, as in CCSDS OEM/OPM, has indices ranging over the members of a state vector, not over the axes of one frame. Position and velocity axes are not the same set even when both are resolved on the same frame, and the units differ per block.

## Why they were excluded

`tensorReferenceFrames` binds each index position to a frame and resolves components on that frame's axes. Both cases break that premise: their indices range over something that is not an axis list. Admitting them means either

- a notion of an ordered basis that is not a frame (so an index position could name a state layout rather than a frame), or
- an `augmented` flag plus rules for what the extra row and column mean,

either of which is a second keyword's worth of machinery.

## Related limitations already stated in the draft

- Symmetries of tensors above rank 2 (minor/major symmetries of an elastic stiffness tensor) are not expressible; those components must each be named individually. This *is* stated in the draft.
- Voigt-packed **compliance** matrices carry factors of 2 and 4 relative to the true tensor components. That is a value-scaling convention, not an indexing one, so no index declaration reaches it. Voigt-packed **stiffness** maps one-for-one and is fine. **Unverified** — recalled, not checked against a source.

## Options

1. Leave out of scope, restore a short scope sentence to the draft so readers are not left to discover the limitation by failing.
2. Add an ordered-basis concept covering both cases.
3. Cover the 4x4 case only, with an `augmented` flag.

## Prerequisite if pursued

A real-world sample and a verified authoritative source for whichever convention is adopted, per repo practice.
